name: Ampère’s law
kicker: Magnetic fields from electric currents · One of Maxwell’s equations
dates: Named for André-Marie Ampère; corrected by Maxwell in the early 1860s
briefing: Ampère’s law says that if you add up the magnetic field all the way around any closed loop, you get a number set by the electric current passing through that loop. Physicists use it to find the magnetic field around a straight wire or inside a coil without hard calculations. James Clerk Maxwell later added a missing piece, and the corrected law became one of the four Maxwell’s equations that describe electricity, magnetism, and light.
answerHtml: Ampère’s law (accept Ampère’s circuital law or Ampère–Maxwell law; prompt on Ampère or Maxwell’s equations; do not accept “Biot–Savart law” or “Faraday’s law”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: This law gives the wrong answer in the gap of a charging capacitor unless it includes a “displacement current” term, which James Clerk Maxwell added in the early 1860s. With that term, a changing electric field makes a magnetic field, just as a current does.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law relating the magnetic field around a closed loop to the electric current passing through the loop.

tossups.p: Using this law with a circular path around a long, straight wire shows that the wire’s magnetic field falls off as one over the distance from the wire. This law plays the same role for magnetism that Gauss’s law plays for electricity, making problems with lots of symmetry easy.
tossups.r: It is applied by drawing an imaginary closed loop around a current. For 10 points, name this law, one of Maxwell’s equations.

tossups.p: Inside a doughnut-shaped coil called a toroid, this law shows that the magnetic field weakens with distance from the doughnut’s center, while outside the coil the field is zero. This law also gives the nearly uniform field inside a long, straight coil called a solenoid.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law, one of Maxwell’s equations, that links a magnetic field to the electric current that makes it.

tossups.p: Outside a coaxial cable whose inner wire and outer sleeve carry equal currents in opposite directions, this law predicts no magnetic field at all, since no net current passes through a loop drawn around the cable. When using this law, only the current that passes through the chosen closed path counts.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law relating the magnetic field around any closed loop to the current through it.

tossups.p: James Clerk Maxwell called this law’s namesake “the Newton of electricity.” That namesake began his experiments in 1820, within weeks of learning that Hans Christian Ørsted had made a compass needle swing using a current.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law, named for a French physicist, about the magnetic field produced by electric currents.

tossups.p: The original form of this law works only for steady currents that do not change over time. Maxwell’s corrected version of this law, together with Faraday’s law of induction, predicted waves of electric and magnetic fields traveling at the speed of light.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law, one of Maxwell’s equations, which says that electric currents produce magnetic fields that circle around them.

tossups.p: The Biot–Savart [“bee-OH suh-VAR”] law gives the same answers as this law, but this law is far easier to use when a problem has a lot of symmetry. The constant in this law, mu-naught, is called the permeability of free space.
tossups.r: This law says that the magnetic field added up around a closed loop is proportional to the current through it. For 10 points, name this law.

tossups.p: This law contains the constant mu-naught, the permeability of free space, which is about four pi times ten to the negative seventh in SI units. That constant multiplies the current that passes through the closed path in this law.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law that links the magnetic field around a loop to the current through it, one of Maxwell’s four equations.

tossups.p: This law’s namesake called his new field of study “electrodynamics.” When using this law around a wire, a right-hand rule gives the direction of the magnetic field: point your thumb along the current, and your fingers curl the way the field circles.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law, one of Maxwell’s equations, about the magnetic fields made by currents.

tossups.p: This law’s namesake also showed in 1820 that two parallel wires carrying currents in the same direction attract each other, a result described by a separate “force law” named for him. James Clerk Maxwell later added a displacement current term to this law.
tossups.r: This law relates the magnetic field around a closed loop to the current inside it. For 10 points, name this law.

tossups.p: This law’s namesake, one of 72 scientists whose names are engraved on the Eiffel Tower, was largely self-taught and became a professor at the École Polytechnique [“ay-KOHL po-lee-tek-NEEK”] in Paris. Maxwell’s corrected version of this law is one of his four famous equations.
tossups.r: This law relates the magnetic field around a closed loop to the current passing through it. For 10 points, name this law.

tossups.p: This law shows that the magnetic field just outside a long, tightly wound solenoid is nearly zero, while inside it equals mu-naught times the number of turns per meter times the current. It works easily around a straight wire, where the field is equally strong all the way around a circle.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law, one of Maxwell’s equations, that links a magnetic field to the current that makes it.

tossups.p: Faraday’s law says that a changing magnetic field makes an electric field, while the corrected form of this law says that a changing electric field makes a magnetic field. That pairing led James Clerk Maxwell to predict that light is an electromagnetic wave.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law relating the magnetic field around a closed loop to the current through the loop.

tossups.p: Applying this law inside a thick wire with current spread evenly across it shows that the magnetic field grows in proportion to the distance from the wire’s center, then weakens outside the wire. The magnetic field lines around the wire form closed circles.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law, one of Maxwell’s equations, that relates a magnetic field to the electric current producing it.

tossups.p: The left side of this law adds up the magnetic field all the way around a closed path, a quantity called the field’s circulation. This law’s namesake proposed that tiny loops of current inside magnets cause their magnetism.
tossups.r: The right side of this law is mu-naught times the current through the path. For 10 points, name this law.

trap.title: Which electromagnetism law?
trap.body: Several laws of electricity and magnetism show up together. This law links the magnetic field circling a closed loop to the current passing through it; Gauss’s law links the electric field through a closed surface to the charge inside; Faraday’s law says a changing magnetic field makes a voltage; and the Biot–Savart law builds up a magnetic field piece by piece. The same French physicist also has a separate force law about parallel wires, and the unit of current carries his name, so saying just “Ampère” earns only a prompt.
trap.fix: Closed loops (Amperian loops), the current enclosed, solenoids, toroids, and Maxwell’s displacement current mean this law. Closed surfaces and enclosed charge mean Gauss’s law; induction, generators, and Lenz’s law mean Faraday’s law; adding up the field from tiny pieces of wire means the Biot–Savart law.
trap.line: Real answer line: Ampère’s law (accept Ampère’s circuital law or Ampère–Maxwell law; prompt on Ampère or Maxwell’s equations; do not accept “Biot–Savart law” or “Faraday’s law”)
